title: Particle Theory
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Particle Theory Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Use particle theory to describe the arrangement of particles in a substance, including the motion of and attraction between particles, and relate this to the properties of the substance (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on the particle theory: solids, liquids and gases, changes of state, diffusion, expansion and conservation of mass. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: All matter is made of moving particles.
key_sub: How close particles are and how fast they move explain each state and change.
body_html:
How to think about it

The particle theory: all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving and attract each other.

  • Solid: particles packed in fixed positions, vibrating. Liquid: close together but moving past each other. Gas: far apart, moving fast.
  • Heating gives particles more energy: they move faster and further apart, so substances expand, melt or boil.
  • Particles do not change size and are not lost in a change of state, so mass stays the same.
Example

Why does a smell spread through a room?

gas particles move randomly

they spread from high to low concentration

Answer: diffusion

Example

Ice melts in a sealed bag. Mass?

no particles are added or lost

Answer: unchanged

Common mistakes

  • Thinking particles themselves expand when heated.
  • Thinking particles in a solid do not move.
  • Thinking mass is lost when a substance melts or evaporates in a sealed container.

faq.a: It is a model that says all matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving, have spaces between them and attract each other.

faq.q: Why do substances expand when heated?
faq.a: The particles gain energy, move faster and take up more space. The particles themselves stay the same size.

faq.q: Why is diffusion faster in gases?
faq.a: Gas particles move faster and have more space between them, so they spread out quickly.

items.q: What does diagram C show?
c: a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a solid: particles far apart and not moving
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: What is Brownian motion?
c: the random jiggling of tiny specks caused by being hit by moving particles
items.e: Evidence for particles.

items.q: How do the particles in a gas move?
c: Move quickly and randomly in all directions.
They do not move at all.
items.e: In a gas, particles are far apart and randomly arranged and move quickly and randomly in all directions.

items.q: Why do gases spread out?
c: Their particles move quickly in all directions.
items.e: Random movement.

items.q: How do the particles in a liquid move?
c: Move quickly and randomly in all directions.
They do not move at all.
items.e: In a liquid, particles are close together but not in fixed positions and slide past one another.

items.q: What happens to the particles when water boils?
c: They gain enough energy to move far apart and escape as a gas.
items.e: The particles themselves stay the same.

items.q: What is diffusion?
c: a solid turning into a liquid
a gas turning into a liquid
the spreading of particles from high to low concentration
items.e: Smells spreading.

items.q: What does diagram B show?
c: a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a gas?
c: They are all touching in a gas.
Closely packed in a fixed, orderly arrangement.
Close together but not in fixed positions.
items.e: In a gas, particles are far apart and randomly arranged and move quickly and randomly in all directions.

items.q: When a solid is heated, what happens to its particles?
c: They vibrate faster and move slightly further apart.
items.e: The particles do not change size; the spaces grow.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
c: They are all touching in a gas.
Closely packed in a fixed, orderly arrangement.
Close together but not in fixed positions.
items.e: In a solid, particles are closely packed in a fixed, orderly arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.

items.q: What does the particle theory say about all matter?
c: It is made of one solid piece.
It is made of tiny particles that are always moving.
Only gases are made of particles.
Its particles only move when heated.
items.e: Particles have spaces between them and attract each other.

items.q: Ice melts in a sealed bag. What happens to the mass?
items.e: No particles are added or lost.

items.q: What is diffusion?
c: the spreading of particles from where there are many to where there are few
items.e: It happens because particles move randomly.

items.q: Why do railway lines have small gaps between sections?
c: The steel expands on hot days and needs room.
items.e: Particles move further apart when heated.

items.q: Why does diffusion happen faster in a gas than in a liquid?
c: Gas particles move faster and are further apart.
items.e: Speed and space.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a liquid?
c: Close together but not in fixed positions.
They are all touching in a gas.
Closely packed in a fixed, orderly arrangement.
items.e: In a liquid, particles are close together but not in fixed positions and slide past one another.

items.q: What is the boiling point of pure water at sea level?
items.e: Water boils at 100 °C.

c: a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other

items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: Which describes what happens to the particles during condensation?
c: They lose energy, slow down and come close together to form a liquid.
They vibrate more strongly and move slightly further apart.
They move more slowly and come closer together.
They gain enough energy to escape from the liquid and move far apart.
items.e: This is how the particle model explains condensation.

items.q: Which state of matter has particles in a regular pattern that vibrate on the spot?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: What is the name for a change from a solid to a liquid?
items.e: Melting, freezing, boiling, condensing and sublimating.

items.q: What is the name for a change from a solid to a gas?
items.e: Melting, freezing, boiling, condensing and sublimating.

What state is nitrogen at −146 °C?
items.e: Below the melting point: solid. Between melting and boiling point: liquid. Above the boiling point: gas.

items.q: Which state of matter has the strongest forces between its particles?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: Which state has particles in fixed positions that vibrate?
items.e: Solids keep their shape.

items.e: Below the melting point: solid. Between melting and boiling point: liquid. Above the boiling point: gas.

items.q: Why can a gas be compressed but a liquid hardly can?
c: Gas particles have large spaces between them.
Gas particles are smaller than liquid particles.
items.e: Pushing the particles closer is easy in a gas.

items.q: Which describes what happens to the particles during boiling?
c: They move more slowly and come closer together.
They lose energy and settle into fixed positions in an orderly arrangement.
They gain enough energy to escape from the liquid and move far apart.
They vibrate more strongly and move slightly further apart.
items.e: This is how the particle model explains boiling.

items.q: What happens to a substance when it is sublimating?
c: It changes from a liquid to a gas.
It changes from a solid to a gas.
It changes from a solid to a liquid.
It changes from a gas to a liquid.
items.e: Changes of state are physical changes.

items.q: Which describes what happens to the particles during freezing?
c: They lose energy and settle into fixed positions in an orderly arrangement.
They gain enough energy to escape from the liquid and move far apart.
They gain energy and move out of their fixed positions, but stay close together.
They move more slowly and come closer together.
items.e: This is how the particle model explains freezing.

items.q: What happens to a substance when it is freezing?
c: It changes from a solid to a liquid.
It changes from a solid to a gas.
It changes from a liquid to a solid.
It changes from a gas to a liquid.
items.e: Changes of state are physical changes.

items.q: Which describes what happens to the particles during contraction of a gas?
c: They move more slowly and come closer together.
They gain energy and move out of their fixed positions, but stay close together.
They lose energy and settle into fixed positions in an orderly arrangement.
They vibrate more strongly and move slightly further apart.
items.e: This is how the particle model explains contraction of a gas.

items.q: What is the name for a change from a liquid to a gas at its boiling point?
items.e: Melting, freezing, boiling, condensing and sublimating.

items.q: Which describes what happens to the particles during expansion of a solid?
c: They lose energy, slow down and come close together to form a liquid.
They vibrate more strongly and move slightly further apart.
They gain enough energy to escape from the liquid and move far apart.
They lose energy and settle into fixed positions in an orderly arrangement.
items.e: This is how the particle model explains expansion of a solid.

items.q: Which state of matter flows and takes the shape of its container but keeps a fixed volume?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: What is the particle model of matter?
c: Only gases are made of particles.
All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving randomly.
Particles are only in living things.
items.e: The particles are too small to see.

items.q: What is the melting point of pure water?
items.e: Ice melts at 0 °C.

items.q: A spray of air freshener can soon be smelt across the classroom. What is the best explanation?
c: The water or air particles stopped moving.
The particles grew bigger and filled the space.
Diffusion: air freshener particles diffused through the air.
The particles were pushed by convection only.
items.e: Particles are always moving randomly, so there is a net movement from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

items.q: What happens to the particles when a gas is cooled?
c: They move more slowly and come closer together.
items.e: The gas contracts.

items.q: What happens to the particles of a solid when it melts?
c: They gain energy and move out of their fixed positions.
items.e: The solid becomes a liquid.

items.q: A tea bag is put into hot water and the colour spreads. What is the best explanation?
c: The particles grew bigger and filled the space.
The particles were pushed by convection only.
The water or air particles stopped moving.
Diffusion: tea particles diffused into the water.
items.e: Particles are always moving randomly, so there is a net movement from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

items.q: Two identical drops of food colouring are added to water at 10 °C and at 80 °C. In which beaker does the colour spread faster?
items.e: At a higher temperature, particles move faster, so diffusion is faster.

items.q: A drop of ink is added to a beaker of still water. After an hour the water is evenly coloured. What is the best explanation?
c: The water or air particles stopped moving.
The particles grew bigger and filled the space.
Diffusion: ink particles moved from a higher to a lower concentration.
The particles were pushed by convection only.
items.e: Particles are always moving randomly, so there is a net movement from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

items.q: What happens to particles when a solid is heated?
items.e: Particles do not expand.

items.q: When ice melts in a sealed bag, what happens to the total mass?
items.e: No particles are added or removed: mass is conserved.

items.q: Two identical drops of food colouring are added to water at 60 °C and at 20 °C. In which beaker does the colour spread faster?
items.e: At a higher temperature, particles move faster, so diffusion is faster.

items.q: Oxygen moves from the air in the lungs into the blood. What is the best explanation?
c: The water or air particles stopped moving.
The particles grew bigger and filled the space.
The particles were pushed by convection only.
Diffusion: oxygen moved from a higher to a lower concentration.
items.e: Particles are always moving randomly, so there is a net movement from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

items.q: Why is the particle model called a model?
c: It is a simple way to explain how matter behaves, based on evidence.
It is a photograph of particles.
items.e: Models are improved when new evidence appears.

items.q: In which state does diffusion happen fastest?
c: it is the same in all states
items.e: Gas particles move fastest and are furthest apart.

items.q: Why does a smell from a barbecue spread across a park?
c: The smell is pushed by light.
Gas particles move randomly and spread out (diffusion).
Smells only travel on hot days.
items.e: Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids.

items.q: Why can a gas be compressed easily but a solid cannot?
c: Gas particles are far apart; solid particles are already closely packed.
items.e: There is a lot of space between gas particles.

items.q: Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas are released at opposite ends of a glass tube. A white ring forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end. What does this show?
c: Ammonia particles diffuse faster because they are lighter.
Both gases diffuse at the same rate.
items.e: Lighter particles move faster at the same temperature.

items.q: What is matter made of?
items.e: The particle model.

items.q: A crystal of potassium manganate(VII) is placed in water. A purple colour slowly spreads. What is the best explanation?
c: The particles were pushed by convection only.
The particles grew bigger and filled the space.
Diffusion: the purple particles moved from a higher to a lower concentration.
The water or air particles stopped moving.
items.e: Particles are always moving randomly, so there is a net movement from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

items.q: What did Robert Brown observe that supports the particle model?
c: Pollen grains in water jiggled randomly.
items.e: Invisible water particles hit the pollen grains from all sides.

items.q: A 40 g steel rod is heated and expands. What happens to the size of its particles?
items.e: Only the spaces between the particles increase.

items.q: The liquid in a thermometer rises when it is warmed. Which explains this?
c: The mass of the substance increases when heated.
The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
The liquid expands as its particles move further apart.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: Power cables sag more on a hot afternoon. Which explains this?
c: The mass of the substance increases when heated.
The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
The cables expand and become longer when heated.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: Concrete roads are built with gaps filled with soft material. Which explains this?
c: The mass of the substance increases when heated.
The concrete can expand on hot days without cracking.
The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: An 80 g copper block is heated and expands. What happens to its density?
c: It increases, because the particles get bigger.
It stays the same, because the mass is the same.
It decreases, because the same mass takes up a larger volume.
It increases, because the mass increases.
items.e: Density = mass ÷ volume. The volume increases while the mass stays the same.

items.q: A 150 g steel rod is heated and expands. What is its mass now?
items.e: No particles are added or removed, so the mass does not change.

items.q: A balloon left in the sun gets bigger. Which explains this?
c: The mass of the substance increases when heated.
The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
The air inside expands as its particles move faster and further apart.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: Gaps are left between sections of a railway track. Which explains this?
c: The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
The steel expands on hot days and needs room to expand.
The mass of the substance increases when heated.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: A block has a mass of 20 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density?
items.e: Density = mass ÷ volume = 20 ÷ 20 = 1 g/cm³.

items.q: A 250 g glass marble is heated and expands. What is its mass now?
items.e: No particles are added or removed, so the mass does not change.

items.q: A 60 g steel rod is heated and expands. What happens to its density?
c: It stays the same, because the mass is the same.
It increases, because the particles get bigger.
It decreases, because the same mass takes up a larger volume.
It increases, because the mass increases.
items.e: Density = mass ÷ volume. The volume increases while the mass stays the same.

items.q: Some chocolate with a mass of 40 g melts completely in a sealed container. What is the mass of the liquid chocolate?
items.e: Mass is conserved in a change of state: no particles are added or lost.

items.q: An 80 g glass marble is heated and expands. What happens to the size of its particles?
items.e: Only the spaces between the particles increase.

items.q: A block has a mass of 100 g and a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density?
items.e: Density = mass ÷ volume = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 g/cm³.

items.q: Some chocolate with a mass of 100 g melts completely in a sealed container. What is the mass of the liquid chocolate?
items.e: Mass is conserved in a change of state: no particles are added or lost.

items.q: A metal lid on a glass jar is held under hot water and then opens easily. Which explains this?
c: The mass of the substance increases when heated.
The metal lid expands more than the glass when heated.
The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: A dented ping-pong ball pops back into shape in hot water. Which explains this?
c: The air particles inside move faster and further apart, pushing the dent out.
The mass of the substance increases when heated.
The particles themselves become bigger when heated.
items.e: Particles move faster and further apart when heated; they do not grow and no new particles form.

items.q: Ella says particles in a hot spoon are bigger. How could you explain the real reason the spoon expands?
c: The particles move more and take up more space, but stay the same size.
The particles really do get bigger.
items.e: Spacing changes, not particle size.

items.q: A 60 g brass key is heated and expands. What is its mass now?
items.e: No particles are added or removed, so the mass does not change.

items.q: A 120 g aluminium ring is heated and expands. What is its mass now?
items.e: No particles are added or removed, so the mass does not change.

items.q: Which state of matter can easily be squashed (compressed)?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
c: Its particles are held in an open pattern with more space between them.
items.e: Water is unusual.

items.q: Which diagram best represents a liquid?
c: particles far apart and randomly arranged
particles touching each other but arranged randomly
particles in neat rows touching each other
items.e: Liquid particles are close but not in fixed positions.

items.q: Why does a balloon left in an air-conditioned room become smaller?
c: The air particles inside move more slowly, so the air contracts.
items.e: Cooling makes a gas contract.

items.q: In Mia's test, what should stay the same?
c: the size of the drop, the amount of water and the containers
items.e: Change only the temperature.

items.q: A syringe of air is sealed and the plunger is pushed in. Why can it move but a syringe full of water cannot?
c: Air particles have large spaces between them; water particles are close together.
items.e: Liquids are almost incompressible.

items.q: How is evaporation different from boiling?
c: Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.
Boiling happens only at the surface.
items.e: Surface vs throughout.

items.q: Ruby weighs a sealed bottle of water (520 g), freezes it, then weighs it again. What will the scale show?
items.e: Mass is conserved in a change of state.

items.q: A substance melts at 63 °C. What does this suggest about it at room temperature (20 °C)?
items.e: Below its melting point.

items.q: Which state of matter has particles far apart that move quickly in all directions?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: A 120 g brass key is heated and expands. What happens to the size of its particles?
items.e: Only the spaces between the particles increase.

items.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: A metal ball just fits through a ring. After the ball is heated, it cannot pass through. Why?
c: The particles of the ball got bigger.
The ball expanded because its particles moved further apart.
The ring shrank when the ball was heated.
items.e: Particles do not change size.

items.q: Jack heats a metal ball that just fits through a ring. After heating it will not pass through. Why?
c: The ring shrank in the heat.
The ball expanded as its particles moved further apart.
items.e: Heat makes most solids expand.

items.q: Which state of matter has particles close together that slide past each other?
items.e: Use the particle model: arrangement, movement and forces.

items.q: Why does a gas exert pressure on the walls of its container?
c: Its particles stick to the walls.
items.e: Particle collisions.

items.q: Why does the smell of cooking spread faster in a hot kitchen than in a cold one?
c: Particles move faster at higher temperatures.
Cold air is denser so smells move faster.
items.e: Diffusion is faster when particles have more energy.
